Furthermore, since the apprehension of an object is not other than consciousness, it is not logical for it to be a mental factor (*caitasika*). Feeling consists in the nature of grasping specific qualities such as pleasure and so forth.

Experience (*paribhoga*) is perception (*saṃjñā*). Furthermore, the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), such as mental attention (*manaskāra*) and so forth, are the activators of consciousness (*vijñāna*) with respect to experience and perception.
Alternatively, experience is feeling (*vedanā*), because it consists in the experiencing of its respective objects and the experiencing of karma that is to be felt as pleasure and so forth.
Thus, feeling (*vedanā*) is "enjoyment" (*upabhoga*) because it experiences the object and its action;
perception (*saṃjñā*) is "discrimination" (*pariccheda*) because it makes the object a distinct mark, serving as the basis for conventional designation;
and formations (*saṃskāra*) are those which set in motion consciousness toward other objects.
In this way, the knowledge of the sovereignty of the mind and so forth resorts to another object;
by the word "and so forth" (ādi), zeal and the other factors are included.
Since it has been stated what [the activity] is, of what kind it is, and for what purpose it proceeds,
he now explains the characteristic of affliction (*saṃkleśa*).
This refers to how the afflictions, karma, and birth— when proceeding as afflictions— constitute the thorough affliction of the world.

That characteristic of affliction is shown to be selfless, yet it arises in saṃsāra from mere unreal imagination; this is explained in detail through the phrases "because of covering, because of planting, because of leading, and because of grasping. This twelve-linked dependent origination is thus presented with reference to the side of active involvement (*pravṛtti*). Furthermore, the statement at the end, "the world is afflicted because of covering," is connected to everything.
By what is there concealment, and how is one afflicted by concealment?
To this it is said: "Because of the obstruction of seeing things as they truly are by ignorance.
For since ignorance is of the nature of non-seeing, when its object is present, the true seeing that has been obscured does not arise.
Therefore, because it obstructs the arising of the vision of reality, ignorance is the obstruction to the vision of reality.
Furthermore, the vision of reality is primarily supramundane knowledge (*lokottara-jñāna*),
since [the subsequent knowledge] arises following upon it.

Because it is attained subsequent to that and because it is the realization of that, the vision of reality (*bhūtadarśana*)—which is based upon it and consists of what is heard (*śrutamaya*), what is reflected upon (*cintāmaya*), and what is cultivated through meditation (*bhāvanāmaya*)—is so designated.
Due to the obstruction of this vision of reality, ignorance (*avidyā*) is the condition for the formative forces (*saṃskāra*); thus, through such concealment, the world is afflicted by ignorance.
Through [the planting of] seeds, the world is afflicted; such is the connection.
To explain by what, where, and whose planting [occurs], it says: "By the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), [there is] the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of consciousness and karma.
In this context, the formative forces are the actions of body, speech, and mind, having the nature of merit, demerit, and the imperturbable.
It is called a "formative force" because it constructs (*abhisaṃskaroti*) a future existence.
The meaning is that it "causes what has been planted to grow.
And it is precisely this [volition] that is expressed by the term *saṃskāra*, not everything.

Furthermore, it becomes capable of fashioning a new existence (*punarbhava*) through the predominance of ignorance (*avidyā*), and not merely by its own existence; therefore, they are called "formations conditioned by ignorance" (*avidyā-pratyayāḥ saṃskārāḥ*).
For it is thus: those [formations] produce renewed existence for one in whom knowledge has not arisen, but not for one in whom knowledge has arisen.
Furthermore, knowledge is not a condition for the formations by its mere predominance alone; rather, they also arise through a general condition.

For just as ignorance, because it is associated with all afflictions, is the general condition for the arising of the afflictions, so too is it the general condition for the arising of the volitions produced by them.

Regarding the arising of meritorious formations (*puṇya-saṃskāra*) which are associated with the aspiration for various states of existence and enjoyments, the ignorance that arises simultaneously with them is the general condition (*sāmānya-pratyaya*). Likewise, regarding the imperturbable formations (*āneñjya*), which arise from the view of liberation within their respective realms, the ignorance that arises simultaneously with them is the general condition; thus, the conditionality of the formations has been explained. Here, by "consciousness" (*vijñāna*), the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) is intended, and not the active consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), because it is impossible for the active consciousnesses to lead one to the place of rebirth through the severance of the continuum.
Because there is no coexistence of the wholesome and the afflicted, and because there is thus no establishment of a latent impression (*vāsanā*) therein by means of formative forces (*saṃskāra*),
[the phrase "of the latent impression of karma" is used].
What, then, is this so-called "latent impression of karma"?
The seed of a future birth is its causal state (*hetubhāva*).
Just as a grain of rice, depending on specific conditions such as soil, dust, and wind, becomes through transformation the cause for the emergence of a sprout, that [rice] is called a "seed.
By the phrase "because of establishing," he expresses "planting" by means of another synonym.
Furthermore, "establishment" (pratiṣṭhāpana) refers to the initial nourishment of that seed within the continuum of consciousness.
For no new seed—whether of a contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomenon—is ever deposited [in a way it did not exist] before.
Thus, the world is afflicted because the formative forces (*saṃskāras*) deposit the seed for renewed existence (*punarbhava*) within consciousness.

It is said: "The world is led astray; by whom and where is it led? To this he replies: "Therefore, by means of consciousness, [there is] leading from the place of birth to the place of arrival. This means that through the continuum of consciousness permeated by karma, there is a leading (*nayana*)—that is, a bringing—from the place of death to the place of rebirth of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) which serves as the seed for renewed existence (*punarbhava*). In this very way, it is demonstrated that the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) are not the condition for the consciousness at the moment of linking (*pratisandhi-vijñāna*), but rather that the consciousness of the prior period of existence itself is the condition for the formative forces.
For it is not logical that an effect should arise from a cause that has already perished.

Since those who have attained the formless absorptions (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) are reborn in the very same place where they pass away, how can there be a "leading to the place of rebirth" in the formless realms? This should be understood according to what is possible, just as in the case of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

To the question, "By what, where, and by the grasping of what is the world afflicted through appropriation? it is said: "By means of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), [there is] the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*).
For name-and-form consists of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).

And these, beginning from the moment of rebirth-linking (*pratisandhi*), exist in the stages of the embryo (*kalala*), the vesicle (*arbuda*), the mass (*ghana*), the flesh (*peśī*), and the limbs (*praśākhā*), while the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) have not yet arisen.
"Name-and-form has consciousness as its condition.
Thus, through the distinction of cultivation, the specific excellence of one belonging to a particular homogeneous class is established, even when other factors are equal;
and that [excellence] has arisen.

The personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) is differentiated according to the distinctions between the classes of beings, such as humans, animals, and so forth; thus, it is said that the personal existence is "appropriated" by name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Alternatively, it appropriates the entire personal existence up until death, because from the very beginning it is established as the causal basis for everything.
Alternatively, since the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) is grasped even by name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) when it is undifferentiated, its differentiation is now being demonstrated;
just as all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are subsumed under the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*),
so too for those of miraculous birth (*aupapāduka*), the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) alone arise with consciousness (*vijñāna*) as their condition.

Therefore, it should be understood that name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) has consciousness (*vijñāna*) as its condition, according to the circumstances. [The commentary states: "The world is afflicted because of filling. By what is there filling, and of what? It is by means of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
The personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) is comprised within name-and-form.

Thus, in the stage of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), because the sense-bases (*āyatana*) such as the eye do not yet exist, the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) is incomplete. Furthermore, even the body-base (*kāyāyatana*) and the mind-base (*manāyatana*) that exist in that stage are likewise incomplete, due to the absence of the perfection of both the supported and the support.
However, in the stage of the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), the supported becomes complete through the manifestation of the eye and the other [senses].
The sense-base of the body (*kāyāyatana*) also becomes complete because of the completion of the eyes and so forth that depend upon it.
How are the eyes and so forth dependent upon it? Because their functioning is bound to it.
The sense-base of the mind (*manāyatana*) also consists of the six consciousnesses.
At that time, it is fully gathered and becomes complete, with its basis fulfilled without remainder;
because of the fulfillment of the major and minor limbs, this occurs during the stage of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
Thus, by way of the fulfillment of the basis through the six sense bases, the world is afflicted.
The connection is: "By what means is the world afflicted?

Contact (*sparśa*) is the discernment (*pariccheda*) of that threefold modification of the sense faculty which arises in accordance with the production of feelings such as pleasure from the coming together of the sense faculty, its object, and consciousness.
For this very reason, because it touches upon the similarity of the modification of the sense faculty by taking on its aspect (*tadākāratayā*), it is called contact (*sparśa*).

Alternatively, contact, conditioned by the six sense bases, produces a threefold modification of the faculties that is conducive to pleasant and other types of feeling. Because it is understood through inclusion, it is said: "by means of feeling, due to enjoyment through craving."
For feeling (*vedanā*) is experienced (*upabhujyate*) by craving (*tṛṣṇā*); the meaning is that it is relished.
Alternatively, the experience of feeling is the experience of meritorious and other types of karma. Or else, "experience" here refers to the direct perception (*anubhava*) of feeling.
Having experienced pleasure and so forth,
the world is afflicted by aversion and attachment there, because of the nourishment of that pleasure and so forth.
Regarding the question "By what, of what, and where is there grasping (*saṅgraha*)?", it is not [the grasping] of a future existence projected by karma alone.

The first chapter [explains]: grasping is that which, by means of the nourishment of the seed of consciousness through the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), and by means of conceptual craving (*tṛṣṇā*)—which, through its specific desire for self-existence (*ātmabhāva*) in all states of rebirth, brings about and casts one into a future existence—is the act of drawing one toward rebirth. Regarding the question "By what, where, and of what is there binding (*nibandhana*)?", he himself provides the answer: it is by means of the appropriations (*upādāna*) that consciousness is established in the objects of desire and so forth, which are conducive to its arising.

By means of the four graspings characterized by desire and attachment, consciousness—projected by karma—ascends to its bond within those states conducive to rebirth, namely: sensual desire, views, rules and observances, and the doctrine of self.
For, under the influence of desire and attachment, consciousness remains fixed there.

Regarding the phrase "because of being directed toward the water of renewed existence," even here, when there is an opportunity for another's question, he himself says: "Because of making manifest the ripening of renewed existence through karma performed by *bhava* (becoming)."

Just as the previously performed karma that leads to renewed existence—which exists in the state of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—is called the "result of maturation" (*vipākaphala*), and because it comes into being through the acquisition of active manifestation (*pravṛtti-lābha*), it becomes oriented toward the projection of existence (*bhava-ākṣepa*);
so too, because existence is brought about by this orientation, the world is afflicted.
As it is said: "The world is afflicted by suffering; the world is afflicted by birth, by old age, and by death."
Thus, when the production of renewed existence from becoming occurs, one is afflicted from the very beginning by the coagulation of consciousness within the semen and blood at the time of conception.

Likewise, one is afflicted by turning about within the space between the mother’s stomach and the intestines. Furthermore, one is afflicted by the distress caused by the mother’s consumption of food and drink, and by the failure to avoid confinement.
The world is afflicted as it goes out by way of a narrow and impure path;

furthermore, once born, the world is afflicted as it is deprived of its two dear things—youth and life—by old age, characterized by baldness, graying hair, and so forth, and by death, characterized by the dissolution of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
It is called "the world" (*jagat*) because it goes.
The meaning is that it goes from a state of homogeneity to a state of momentariness.

"It is afflicted" means that within the three realms, through a succession of moments, it is tormented by birth, old age, sickness, death, and so forth, in a state of constant flux; such is the meaning.
Others say that "it is afflicted" means that it is not purified.

Thus, this *Madhyāntavibhāga-sūtra-bhāṣya-ṭīkā* explains that the twelve-linked dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), characterized by affliction (*saṃkleśa*) due to concealment (*chādana*), constitutes the adversary to purification (*vyavadāna*) through eleven aspects, beginning with [the aspect of] "the sequence of the terms ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth," because each preceding member gives rise to each succeeding one. Furthermore, in how many ways is affliction (*saṃkleśa*) briefly demonstrated by this twelve-linked dependent origination? For this reason, it is said: "This twelve-linked dependent origination is threefold, twofold, and also sevenfold as affliction."
The word "iti" has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
"Defilement of afflictions" (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*) means that affliction itself is the defilement.
Likewise, there is the defilement of karma and the defilement of birth.

For affliction (*kleśa*), when it arises, is a defilement (*saṃkleśa*) because it causes harm to both oneself and others. As it has been said: "One who is attached and overcome by passion intends for his own harm; he intends for the harm of others; he intends for the harm of both.
The same should be understood for hatred and delusion as well."
Karma and birth are also afflictions because they cause the process of affliction to proceed;
for it is through the sovereignty of the afflictions that karma projects birth.

For one who has seen the truths, even though karma exists, there is no further projection of existence (*punarbhava*). Because the seed of future existence is made to become existence through the manifestation of the afflictions (*kleśa*), and because of the binding of the connection to rebirth for one whose mind is afflicted, the affliction of birth is the cause [of the cycle].
For this very reason, an Arhat does not undergo rebirth due to the absence of an afflicted mind.
Furthermore, wholesome and unwholesome karma is a defilement because it causes exhaustion of body and mind and because it yields maturation in the future.
Birth, too, is a defilement because it is the locus of all calamities; thus, defilement is threefold due to the twofold division of its cause.
The defilement of afflictions (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*) consists of ignorance, craving, and grasping, as these three have the nature of affliction.
The defilement of karma consists of both *saṃskāra* and *bhava*, because both have karma as their essence.
However, this is the distinction:
*saṃskāra* is karma in its state as essential nature (*svarūpa*), whereas *bhava* is karma in its state as a seed (*bīja*).

The defilement of birth consists of the remaining members—consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), birth (*jāti*), and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*)—because these are comprised within birth. Defilement is twofold, distinguished by its causes:
the defilement of cause consists of those members whose intrinsic nature is affliction (*kleśa*) and karma.
"And the defilement of the fruit [is comprised] by the remaining members.

In that regard, karma and the afflictions constitute the "defilement of the cause" because they are engaged in producing birth—which consists of the factors from consciousness up to feeling, as well as birth characterized by old age, death, and so forth.
And the "defilement of the fruit" consists of the remaining factors, consciousness and the rest, because they are the fruit of karma and the afflictions.

Furthermore, that very same dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) as defilement (*saṃkleśa*) is sevenfold; it is a sevenfold cause because it is the cause of perversion (*viparyāsa*), projection (*ākṣepa*), leading (*upanayana*), grasping (*parigraha*), enjoyment (*upabhoga*), attraction (*ākārṣaṇa*), and agitation (*udvega*).
Among these, ignorance (*avidyā*) is the cause of perversion;
for one who has fallen into ignorance, due to delusion regarding reality (*tattva*), one becomes perverted by perceiving the impermanent as permanent and so forth.

"The projecting cause is the formative forces (*saṃskāra*)," because the seed of birth, consisting of four factors, is deposited within consciousness. Consciousness is the "conveying cause" because it conveys one who has passed away from here to the sphere of rebirth.
Name-and-form and the six sense-bases are the cause of appropriation;
for once one has been brought forth, the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*) is appropriated by means of name-and-form and the six sense-bases.
Previously, appropriation was stated to be by name-and-form alone with reference to the womb-born (*jarāyuja*) and other modes of birth.
Now, having established the section on spontaneous birth (*upapāduka*), it is stated that there is also inclusion by means of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
Alternatively, by means of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the inclusion of the mere personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) at its very inception was intended;
here, however, [the inclusion] is of both the incomplete and the complete [existence], so there is no contradiction.
"Contact and feeling are the cause of experience," because through experience accompanied by its causes, one experiences the maturation of wholesome and unwholesome karma.
"Craving, grasping, and becoming are the cause of attraction."
Experiencing the ripening of karma, the fool craves each and every sensation.
With craving thus intensified, through the craving for union with and separation from those sensations, he grasps at sense-pleasures and the rest.

Due to that grasping, his previously existing karma pertaining to rebirth—which existed in the state of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—undergoes transformation; having attained activity for the purpose of yielding its projected ripening, it becomes *bhava* (becoming).

And since that [volitional formation] is drawn forth and brought face-to-face for the production of renewed existence projected by those formations, craving, grasping, and becoming are the "cause of attraction.

Alternatively, because the latencies of karma—whether of sensual desire or another type—are brought face-to-face through the power of craving, craving, grasping, and becoming are the cause of attraction.
Birth, aging, and death are the "cause of agitation."

For it is thus: through the projection of birth, one experiences in various classes of beings the suffering of birth, aging, and death, as well as other sufferings— sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair— in their infinite varieties.

In this context, by the threefold designation of defilement (*saṃkleśa*), it is shown that afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma are the common and uncommon causes of birth. For affliction is the common cause of the sprout of birth, like the earth and other elements; whereas karma is the uncommon cause, like the seed is for the sprout, because there is a differentiation of births according to the differentiation of that [karma].
Alternatively, it is not that there are three sections here consisting of the past, the future, and the middle;
rather,
it demonstrates that they are the results of karma and afflictions.
By this twofold designation, it is shown that this is merely cause and effect, and that there is no other agent or experiencer who becomes defiled here.
Alternatively, it shows that karma and afflictions alone are the cause, because one observes that the existence or non-existence of birth follows from the existence or non-existence of those two;
therefore, birth is indeed their fruit.
Therefore, there is neither cause nor fruit [independently];
rather, it demonstrates that in all cases it is a state consisting of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandhika-avasthā*).

Furthermore, by means of the sevenfold exposition of causes, dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is shown to be twofold: characterized by projection (*ākṣepa-lakṣaṇa*) and characterized by actualization (*abhinirvṛtti-lakṣaṇa*).

Therein, dependent origination characterized by projection is demonstrated by seven members, because of the demonstration of that by which one is projected, how one is projected, and that which is projected. Dependent origination characterized by actualization is demonstrated by five members: [the demonstration] of that which has been projected—by what its actualization occurs, how it is actualized, and what that actualization is—and of the fact that this very actualization is nothing but suffering.
By what is one projected?
By the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) conditioned by ignorance (*avidyā*).
How so?
Through the perverted perceptions of delusion regarding reality and so forth, one forms wholesome, unwholesome, and imperturbable volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
How, then, is [consciousness] projected by these volitional formations?
Because it nourishes the seed of consciousness and establishes the potential for rebirth,
what is projected?
It is name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling pertaining to renewed existence, as appropriate.
Thus, by what is that which has been projected brought about?

It is brought about by the craving that arises here in dependence upon the feeling produced from the previous projection according to the sequence already described, and by means of grasping (*upādāna*) conditioned by that craving.
How is it brought about by that?

The first section concerns the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of consciousness, because by means of that [consciousness], the karma of one existing in a particular state is brought into existence. For the manifold latent impressions of karmic consciousness persist, being thoroughly permeated by diverse formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and being grasped through specific types of appropriation (*upādāna*).
That by which rebirth occurs from this [existence] is called "existence" (*bhava*) here.
What, then, is that "actualization" (*abhinirvṛtti*)?
It is the final birth of that projected [continuum], beginning with name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Furthermore, when that [craving] exists, what is the disadvantage?

It is aging and death, resulting from the loss of beloved youth and life. In this context, however, the reason for leading [to the conclusion] is not without purpose, because it eliminates the knowledge of the arising of existence through birth by cutting off the possibility of death.

This entire affliction proceeds from unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*), because affliction has the mind and mental factors as its basis. For it has been said: "Unreal imagination consists of the mind and mental factors belonging to the three realms."

Furthermore, regarding the summary meaning (*piṇḍārtha*) of the construction of the unreal (*abhūtaparikalpa*): the detailed exposition of the meaning is for the sake of easy comprehension, whereas the exposition of the summary meaning is for the sake of non-forgetfulness.
Therefore, two types of meaning have been explained here.
The characteristic of existence is: "unreal imagination exists.
The characteristic of non-existence is: "this [object] is not found therein.
The specific characteristic is that which arises appearing as objects, sentient beings, a self, and representations.
Regarding "consciousness":

it consists of the characteristic of inclusion—the imagined (*parikalpita*), the dependent (*paratantra*), and the perfected (*pariniṣpanna*)—and the characteristic of the means for entering the characteristic of non-existence, such as: "Based upon perception, non-perception arises," and so forth.
The characteristic of differentiation is: "The imagination of the unreal consists of mind and mental factors belonging to the three realms.
The characteristic of synonyms is: "Therein, the perception of objects is consciousness (*vijñāna*), while that which pertains to their specific qualities is the mental factors (*caitasika*).
The characteristic of activity is: "One is the consciousness as condition (*pratyaya-vijñāna*); the second is that which pertains to experience (*aupabhogika*)."
"The characteristic of affliction is through concealing, planting, leading, and grasping," and so forth.

In the *Madhyāntavibhāga-sūtra-bhāṣya-ṭīkā*, it is stated that after the ninefold characteristic of unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*) has been explained, the manner in which emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is to be known is then indicated.
What is the connection here?
This has been asserted by him: that there is the unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*) and emptiness (*śūnyatā*);

that purification is preceded by affliction; and that the determination of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is based upon the realization of phenomena. Therefore, immediately after the exposition of the unreal imagination, he explains how emptiness is to be understood, stating in detail: "Now, its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and its synonyms (*paryāya*)," and so forth. Among these, the characteristic of emptiness consists in the negation of both existence and non-existence, because it pervades all its various divisions.
A synonym (*paryāya*) is another name.
The meaning of a synonym is the ground for the application of that synonym in accordance with its actual referent;
this is because, like space, it possesses an undifferentiated characteristic.

Even in the state of non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpa*), there is a distinction based on the difference between the states of conjunction with and disjunction from adventitious secondary afflictions (*āgantukopakleśa*).
Furthermore, there is another sixteenfold distinction based on the superimposition (*samāropa*) of persons (*pudgala*) and phenomena (*dharma*).
The means of proof (*sādhana*) refers to the reasoning (*yukti*) for demonstrating the various classifications of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Furthermore, what is the reason that emptiness must be understood through these modes?
Because it is the object of purification, it should be understood by those seeking purification according to its characteristics (*lakṣaṇataḥ*).
And it should be understood according to its synonyms (*paryāyataḥ*) so that there is no confusion regarding the various explanations of its synonyms.

It should be understood from the perspective of synonyms for the sake of understanding the meaning of those synonyms; from the perspective of emptiness for the sake of establishing that it is the object of purification; from the perspective of differentiation for the sake of generating effort toward the abandonment of afflictions, based on the principle that its purification occurs through the removal of defilements; and also from the perspective of the means of differentiation, because even when there is no occasion for realizing the proof of differentiation, one can easily comprehend the differentiation [through such means].
How is the characteristic to be understood?
Since the characteristic was mentioned first, it is therefore asked about first.
One should understand that the characteristic of emptiness is the non-existence of existence and the existence of non-existence.

Because this [duality]— both the grasped and the grasper— is of an imagined nature within the unreal imagination (abhūtaparikalpa) or by means of the unreal imagination, it lacks existence as a real entity.
The existence of that very non-existence of duality is the defining characteristic of emptiness.

Furthermore, in accordance with the *kārikā*, the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) here should be understood as being elided in the expression "the existence of non-existence" (*abhāvasya bhāvaḥ*). This is because it constitutes the first chapter.
What are these two?
The self-nature of non-existence (abhāva) is indeed existent;
otherwise, for that whose existence would be truly existent, its non-existence would not exist as a reality.
Therefore, he said: "Thus, emptiness is demonstrated to have the characteristic of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, and not the characteristic of the form of existence."

Since the word "non-existence" (abhāva) expresses the negation of existence (bhāva), its meaning is understood even in the absence of the word "existence"; therefore, the word "existence" is redundant here. [Response:
It is not redundant.

For when it is pointed out that "the non-existence of duality is the characteristic of emptiness," the non-existence of duality is understood here as being independent, like the non-existence of a hare's horn, and not as having the nature of a universal property (dharmatā) like suffering and so forth.
Therefore, it is said: "The non-existence of duality is emptiness;

and the existence of that non-existence within the unreal imagination is [also] emptiness. Because this emptiness is grasped as having the characteristic of the existence of non-existence, the intrinsic nature of the imagined (parikalpita) is thus fully described.

Alternatively, because the word "non-existence" (abhāva) has a general sense—as in the phrases "the state of compassion" (*dayābhāva*) and "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*)—it is not understood which specific kind of non-existence is intended. Therefore, in order to demonstrate absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), it is said: "The existence of the state of compassion within the construction of the unreal" (*abhūtaparikalpe dayābhāvasya bhāvaḥ*).
For it is not logical for antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) or non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) to be perceived elsewhere than in their own substratum.
Furthermore, since mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) depends upon both relata, it is not logical for it to have only a single locus.
Therefore, it is made known that emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is precisely the absolute non-existence of the grasped and the grasper, which are characterized by the apprehension of entities.
If emptiness is of the nature of non-existence, how can it be called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)?
It is so called because it is the object of supreme knowledge (*paramajñāna*), just as impermanence is, and not because it is a substantial entity.

Moreover, even though it has the nature of non-existence (*abhāvasvabhāva*), it is not [simply] non-existent; for that which is its very state of being non-existent is neither an existence nor a non-existence.
How is it not an existence?
Because it is the absence of duality.
For if there were existence, there would be no absolute non-existence of anything, nor would there be the nature of unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa-dharmatā*).
How could it not be non-existence?

Because the existence of the non-existence of compassion (*dayābhāva*)—for when there is the non-existence of compassion—the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of that non-existence of compassion does not become non-existent.
And without that [emptiness], there would be mere non-existence, just as with the dharmas of unreal imagination, such as impermanence and suffering.
For, due to the delusions of sentient beings, the nature of an entity—which is superimposed as being permanent and pleasant—is neither an existence nor a non-existence.
To the question, "If emptiness is the dharma of unreal imagination, should it be said to be different from it or not different? he says: "And this is the characteristic of emptiness."
It is precisely the very nature of non-existence;
or rather, existence itself consists in the negation of non-existence.
Therefore, the characteristic of emptiness is not separate from the imagination of the unreal.
If there were a distinctness [between them], it would not be tenable to say that "the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is other than phenomena (dharma)"; furthermore, it would be illogical.
Because its characteristic would be distinct from phenomena and so forth, the true nature of phenomena would itself become another phenomenon, just like any other phenomenon different from it.
Furthermore, one dharma cannot be the *dharmatā* (essential nature) of another dharma;
for that [second dharma] would also require another dharma through further effort, leading to an infinite regress,
as in the cases of impermanence (*anityatā*) and suffering (*duḥkhatā*).
Just as impermanence is not other than impermanent things, so too suffering is not other than what is suffering; likewise, emptiness is not other than what is empty.
If there were identity [between them], there would be no object for purification, nor would there be a universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
Purification (*viśuddhi*) is the path (*mārga*), because one is purified by means of it.
Because it is not other than the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena, the path—like the specific characteristic of phenomena—is not an object of cognition (*ālambana*).
Therefore, even a universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is not tenable, because it is not other than the specific characteristic.
Furthermore, since that [universal] would also possess mutual differentiation just like the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of phenomena, its status as a universal is lost.
Alternatively, because the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) is not different from that [entity], there is an absence of difference in the essential nature of the entity;
and consequently, there is also an absence of the universal (sāmānya),
since the characteristic of a universal depends upon difference.
Alternatively, because it is that which is to be purified, the object is called the "object of purification.
An entity with its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), when taken as an object, does not bring about purification,
for that would entail the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) that all sentient beings are already purified.
If it is inexpressible in terms of being either identical to or different [from the aggregates],
how is it that the doctrine of the Nirgranthas is not being relied upon?
For whoever explains the existence of a person (*pudgala*) as being either identical to or different from the aggregates relies upon the doctrine of the Nirgranthas.
But since emptiness is not a [positive] entity, this fault does not arise.

And thus, this emptiness has been fully described as having the characteristic of non-existence, the characteristic of the nature of being without intrinsic being, as being without characteristics, and as having a characteristic that is free from both identity and difference.
The first chapter: The characteristic of emptiness has been explained.

Now its synonyms are stated: Suchness (*tathatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the signless (*animitta*), the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), and the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*)—these, in brief, are the synonyms of emptiness.
Thus:
a synonym (*paryāya*) is the mention of different words for a single meaning. It is called a synonym because it expresses the same object through a synonymous term.
And by these designations, emptiness itself is indicated throughout the various sections.
Furthermore, this primary pentad of synonyms has been stated in the verse; likewise, other synonyms not mentioned here should be understood from the scriptures (*pravacana*).

For example: non-conceptuality, the non-discriminative realm (*avikalpaka-dhātu*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), ineffability, cessation (*nirodha*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), nirvāṇa, and so forth.
How is the meaning of these synonyms to be understood? That is now explained:
those words are not merely conceptual constructs.
What then? They are [called] "according to their meaning" (anvartha).

Because they are non-otherwise, because they are non-erroneous, because they are the cessation of that [error], because they are the domain of the Noble Ones, and because they are the cause of the noble dharmas, these are the meanings of the synonyms in their respective order.
Thus, in this context, "suchness" (*tathatā*) is used in the sense of being non-otherwise; that is to say, it means the sense of being unchanging.
It is stated that because it always remains as such through the revelation of reality, it is called "reality."
The meaning is that because it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it does not undergo transformation at any time;
it is the "limit of reality" (*bhūtakoṭi*) in the sense of being non-erroneous. "Reality" (*bhūta*) means truth, that which is non-perverted.
The "limit" (koṭi) is the boundary (paryanta).
Since there is no other object of knowledge beyond it, it is called the "limit of reality" (bhūtakoṭi), meaning the boundary of what is real.
How is suchness (tathatā) the limit of the knowable?

Because it is the objective domain of knowledge for the purification of the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), it is in the sense of being non-erroneous; that is, by way of the meaning of neither superimposition nor denial.
He states the reason for this very point: "because error has no real object.
For error is indeed conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Because it is not an object of conceptual construction, it is not a basis for error;
because it is contrary to signs, it is signless (*animitta*). Here, "signless" means being contrary to signs.
To demonstrate this, he says: "Because of the absence of all signs.
Emptiness is called signless because it is empty of all signs, whether conditioned or unconditioned;
it is signless because of the absence of all signs.

The signless (*animitta*) itself is the signless; it is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) because it is the domain of noble knowledge (*āryajñāna*). "Ultimate truth" means the object (*artha*) of that supreme, supramundane (*lokottara*) knowledge.
Demonstrating this very point, [the author] says: "because it is the domain of supreme knowledge."
It is the *dharmadhātu* because it is the cause of the noble qualities (*āryadharma*).
By the word "dharma" are meant the noble qualities beginning with right view and ending with the knowledge of right liberation;
since it is the cause of these, it is called a *dhātu*.
Elucidating this very point, he says: "Because the noble dharmas arise from that as their objective support.

Although the word *dhātu* (element) also functions to denote that which maintains its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*), he states that here the meaning of *dhātu* is the sense of "cause" (*hetu*).
For example, as in "gold element" (*suvarṇadhātu*) or "copper element" (*tāmradhātu*).
Furthermore, other synonyms mentioned in the intermediate sections should also be explained according to their own meaning by this same sequence.
Since emptiness consists in the absence of the apprehended and the apprehender, [the author], not conceiving of any differentiation therein, asks;

or else, because it was stated that "differentiation is to be understood immediately after the meaning of the synonyms," he asks immediately following that explanation: "How is the differentiation of emptiness to be understood?"
Unreal imagination is defilement; when that is abandoned, there is purity. Thus, even at the times of defilement and purity, there is nothing other than emptiness that is either defiled or purified.

Therefore, in order to demonstrate that it is emptiness itself that is defiled and purified during the times of defilement and purity, he says: "It is both defiled and pure. This is its differentiation.
Not understanding when it is defiled and when it is stainless, one asks: "When is it defiled? When is it pure?"
"Defiled with impurity, impure, and pure"—this is the detailed explanation.
With reference to the non-transformation and transformation of the basis (*āśraya*), it is established as being "with impurity" (*samala*) when it has been abandoned [of defilements].

For those ignorant ones whose mental continuums are stained by the afflictions such as attachment due to their adherence to the grasped and the grasper, and for whom emptiness does not manifest because of the faults of non-comprehension and miscomprehension—in relation to them, it is established as "defiled with impurity."

—The First Chapter: For those noble ones whose minds are non-erroneous due to the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), emptiness (*śūnyatā*) manifests continuously like space, free from dust; with respect to them, it is said to be "devoid of stains.

Thus, the perception of defilement (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*viśuddhi*) regarding emptiness is relative; by virtue of its intrinsic luminosity (*prakṛtiprabhāsvaratva*), it is not stained in its own nature.
If it were stained, it would be subject to change (*vikāra*), and so forth; for indeed, a difference in states is never observed without change.
Since transformation is permeated by arising and perishing, he asks: "How is it that [emptiness], being characterized by transformation, is not impermanent?
There is no transformation other than that from the state of affliction to the state of purification of emptiness.
In reality, because adventitious defilements are removed from the state that does not undergo any change in its intrinsic nature,
purity is asserted to be like the purification of the elements, gold, and space.
Thus, for that reason, it is not impermanent.

For just as the elements of water, gold, and space—because their nature is eternal—are not possessed of the nature of impurity even when they appear to have adventitious stains, and because they possess natural purity upon the removal of those adventitious stains even without undergoing a change in their essential nature; so too, emptiness is defiled by adventitious stains while its own form remains unaltered, and it becomes pure when those [stains] are removed.

For one who establishes that very same entity—which was previously characterized by affliction—as having a subsequently pure intrinsic nature, that [entity] undergoes transformation through a change in its intrinsic nature; however, in that case, both [affliction and purity] would be adventitious.
Therefore, such an entity does not touch upon the nature of transformation.
Since the various classifications must be explained within the section on the detailed exposition, he says: "This is another classification: emptiness is sixteenfold."
It is of sixteen kinds according to the distinction of entities;
for there is no difference in the essential nature of non-existence itself.
These sixteen kinds of emptiness are set forth in the *Prajñāpāramitā*, from "internal emptiness" up to "emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence."
This very [classification] should be understood in brief.
This is for the purpose of abandoning attachment and clinging to that [world].
For attachment and clinging to that indeed constitute an obstacle to attaining the liberation of Buddhahood;
immediately after that, there is the consumption of that food.
Immediately after that, the body, which is the substratum for both of those, must be contemplated;
and the receptacle world, which is the support for that body as its substratum, must be contemplated.
This is for the purpose of turning back the grasping at "mine" and the attachment to self, since [the world] serves as an aid to the enjoyer.
These are the four kinds of entities;
their emptiness is called the "emptiness of entities.
In that regard, friend, the emptiness of the three begins with the internal sense bases.
And these [bases] range from the eye up to the mind.

Because there is no experiencer other than them, and because the world observes the engagement of the eyes and so forth in the enjoyment of objects, the conceit of being an experiencer is attributed by the world to the eyes and so forth; therefore, the emptiness of the bases such as the eye is called the "emptiness of the experiencer.
The "emptiness of the experienced" refers to the external [objects].
And those [objects], beginning with form and ending with mental phenomena (*dharma*),
are called "food" because one enjoys them as objective entities. Therefore, the emptiness of the bases of action is called the "emptiness of food."

Because that body exists as an inseparable state between those two— the enjoyer and the enjoyed— it is called a "body" (*śarīra*). Therefore, its emptiness is the foundational entity, the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*),
because it is known as the supporting basis for all sentient beings.
For this very reason, it is said: "Because of its extreme vastness, its emptiness is called 'great emptiness' (*mahāśūnyatā*).
The word "entity" (*vastu*) is connected to each [of the four] individually.

When that Bodhisattva practitioner is thus attending with a conceptual mental engagement (*savikalpamanaskāra*) upon the emptiness of the four kinds of knowable entities, another grasping of signs (*nimittagrāha*) arises.

“By means of this knowledge of emptiness (*śūnyatājñāna*), the internal and external sense-bases (*āyatana*) and so forth are seen as empty. In that regard, the attachment to the grasped and the grasper, as well as the notion that ‘this has been seen by means of that knowledge of emptiness’—this very conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is the form of ultimate reality (*paramārthākāra*). Through the elimination (*vibhāvanā*) of these two types of conceptualization, which are the causes of error on the stages of yoga (*yogabhūmi*), the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatāśūnyatā*) and the emptiness of the ultimate (*paramārthaśūnyatā*) are taught respectively by way of the abolition of the forms of knowledge (*jñānākāra*). Or rather, because it has emptiness as its object, knowledge itself is called ‘emptiness’ therein.”
The first section on the apprehended: Emptiness by way of the absence of an apprehender is the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*).

Furthermore, the internal sense bases and so forth are empty of that very knowledge (*jñāna*) as it perceives them; this is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) here. Emptiness in that aspect is the emptiness of the ultimate (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
What is the reason?

For the ultimate truth is empty of the imagined nature; yet this too is another grasping at signs (*nimittagrāha*), which becomes an affliction to the cultivation of emptiness— that very emptiness for the sake of which the bodhisattva practices it—
since the nature of an entity is superimposed upon it.

In order to cultivate that [non-conceptual wisdom], the various types of emptiness, beginning with the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*) and ending with the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*), have been taught.
And for what purpose does one practice?
For the sake of attaining the pure [qualities] and so forth.
The meaning is that one practices emptiness for the sake of purifying all phenomena; that is, one cultivates emptiness. The path and nirvāṇa are wholesome, whether conditioned or unconditioned.
The application of both of these is, respectively, "conditioned emptiness" (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*) and "unconditioned emptiness" (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*),
as well as "always for the benefit of sentient beings"—
that is, "I must act for the benefit of all sentient beings in every way and at all times."
That is the emptiness of emptiness and the ultimate emptiness;
and for the sake of not abandoning cyclic existence,
and for the sake of sentient beings, cyclic existence must not be forsaken by me.
Indeed, one who abandons cyclic existence alone does not attain awakening;
such a person remains on the level of a śrāvaka.
For them, emptiness is the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end.

But for what purpose is emptiness taught for that [receptivity]? To this he says: "Not seeing the emptiness of saṃsāra, which is without beginning or end, one becomes weary and abandons saṃsāra"—this is for the sake of inexhaustible virtue and for *nirvāṇa* without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*). He explains that the root of merit is inexhaustible because it does not scatter even in *nirvāṇa* without remainder; thus, the commentary on the *Madhyāntavibhāga-sūtra-bhāṣya*, which states "he does not relinquish it," is established.

If it is so for the past [moments] of the *dharmakāya* which possesses outflows (*sāsrava*), then how is it that there is a *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*? Since the *vipākakāya* no longer exists, yet the state free from outflows (*anāsrava-bhāva*) of the Blessed Buddhas does not undergo the cessation of its continuum even in the *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*—this is the established tenet (*siddhānta*).
Therefore, that is called the emptiness of non-dispersal (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*).

And for the sake of the purification of the lineage (*gotra*), its emptiness is *prakṛti-śūnyatā* (emptiness of intrinsic nature). Here he states the reason: "For the lineage is the intrinsic nature."
From where is this known? To this he says: "intrinsic" (*svābhāvikam*).
The meaning is that it is intrinsic, existing from beginningless time, and not accidental.
How so?
In beginningless saṃsāra, some things are sentient and some are insentient;
likewise, here too, some sixfold sense-bases (ṣaḍāyatana) belong to the lineage of the Buddhas, while others belong to the lineage of the Śrāvakas and so forth.
Nor is this lineage accidental, because it has been transmitted through an unbroken succession from the beginningless past, just like the distinction between the sentient and the insentient.

"All sentient beings are the domain of the Tathāgata. Others say that "domain" (*gocara*) here should be understood as such; [it refers to] "for the sake of the primary and secondary marks. The emptiness-characteristic of the major marks of a Great Man, together with their secondary marks, is called "emptiness.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva applies himself for the purification of the Buddha-qualities.
Because of the statement "he resorts" (*prapadyate*), this term is connected to everything that follows.
A bodhisattva resorts [to these practices] for the sake of attaining the two kinds of merit;
and a bodhisattva always resorts [to them] for the welfare of sentient beings.
Thus... [one asks] "Of which Buddha-qualities? To this he says: "Of the powers, the fearlessnesses, the unique qualities (*āveṇika*), and so forth.

He practices with the thought: "In brief, I must strive for the attainment of all Buddha-qualities. Therefore, he meditates upon that [emptiness], thinking: "Emptiness is the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmaśūnyatā*)."
What, then, is cultivation?
It is the unimpeded engagement of knowledge with respect to the object of knowledge.
In this way, first of all, the establishment of the fourteen [emptinesses], beginning with internal emptiness and ending with the emptiness of all phenomena, is to be understood.

What, then, is emptiness (*śūnyatā*) regarding the enjoyer and so forth? To this he says: "The non-existence of the person (*pudgala*) and of phenomena (*dharma*) therein is emptiness; the actual existence of that non-existence is another emptiness beyond it."
Thus,
in that regard, the absence of a person (pudgala) and of phenomena (dharma) within the aforementioned experiencer and so forth is emptiness;
furthermore, the actual existence of that very absence is also emptiness.
In this context, the non-existence of the person (*pudgala*) and phenomena (*dharma*) is the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*).
The actual existence of that non-existence is the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*).

To the question, "How are these two types of internal emptiness established at the end? he says: "Because of the instruction on the characteristics of emptiness. Furthermore, for what purpose is there an instruction on the characteristics of emptiness? He says: "For the purpose of avoiding, respectively, the superimposition (*samāropa*) of the person and phenomena, as well as the denial (*apavāda*) of their emptiness."
In order to avoid the superimposition (*samāropa*) of persons and phenomena, he establishes the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*);
and in order to avoid the denial (*apavāda*) of that emptiness, he establishes the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence (*abhāvasvabhāva-śūnyatā*).
For if the emptiness of non-existence were not taught, it would follow that there is indeed the existence of phenomena and persons whose forms are merely imagined.

If the emptiness of intrinsic nature were not stated as non-existence, it would follow that emptiness itself is non-existent. And because of that [non-existence], the existence of the person (*pudgala*) and of phenomena (*dharma*) would occur as before.

In this regard, internal sense-bases (*āyatana*), which have the nature of maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) and are considered by the ignorant to be the experiencer—therein, the non-existence of the person who is the experiencer, of the imagined characteristics such as the eye and so forth, and the actual existence of that non-existence, is "internal emptiness" (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*).

External emptiness (*bāhya-śūnyatā*) is the non-existence of the enjoyer—the self—and of the objects of enjoyment, such as form and so forth, which are of the nature of appearances and are conceived by the foolish as external sense-bases (*bāhyāyatana*); it is also the actual existence of that non-existence.

Internal-and-external emptiness (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*) is the non-existence of the person (*pudgala*) who is the enjoyer within the body, of the objects such as form and so forth as they are imagined by foolish people, and of the body itself; it is also the actual existence of that non-existence.

In the container-world (*bhājanaloka*), the non-existence of the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*), the non-existence of its imagined nature (*parikalpitasvabhāva*), and the actual existence of that non-existence constitute the Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*). Furthermore, the non-existence—respectively—of the knowledge of emptiness (*śūnyatājñāna*) which has the ultimate as its form yet possesses the form of a knower and grasps a subject, of the person (*pudgala*) whose characteristic is imagined, and of the ultimate aspect of the knowledge of emptiness; and the actual existence of that non-existence, are respectively the Emptiness of Emptiness (*śūnyatāśūnyatā*) and the Emptiness of the Ultimate (*paramārthaśūnyatā*).

Now, regarding those objects for which the bodhisattva practices— ranging from the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) up to all the qualities of a Buddha (*sarvabuddhadharma*) as the purpose of the bodhisattva’s accomplishment—

the non-existence of the person (*pudgala*) and of phenomena (*dharma*) characterized by conceptual construction, as well as the existence of that very non-existence, are respectively [designated] as "the emptiness of the conditioned" up to "the emptiness of all phenomena.
For it is thus:
There is no owner or agent of the conditioned, nor is there a person (*pudgala*) as imagined by foolish people, nor is there the conditioned itself [as such].

In brief, these sixteen emptinesses, which are not shared by the Śrāvakas, have been taught for the sake of counteracting all grasping at conceptual constructions and for the sake of explaining all the intentions of the Tathāgata’s teachings.
Here, the Blessed One has shown the objective domain of emptiness, the intrinsic nature of emptiness, and the purpose of the cultivation of emptiness.
In this context, the object of emptiness consists of all things from the enjoyer and so forth up to the qualities of a Buddha.
Furthermore, its demonstration is for the purpose of making known that emptiness pervades all phenomena.
The intrinsic nature of emptiness is the intrinsic nature of non-existence, and the intrinsic nature of the existence of non-existence.

Furthermore, the demonstration of the intrinsic nature of emptiness is for the purpose of making known that it consists in the departure from all views by means of the antidote to superimposition and denial. The purpose of the cultivation of emptiness begins with "for the sake of attaining the two-fold merit" and extends to the limit of "for the purification of the Buddha-qualities. Moreover, that demonstration is for the purpose of showing that the excellence of the perfection of the form-body and the dharma-body for oneself and others arises precisely from the cultivation of emptiness.

Thus, the classification of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) should be understood as follows: it is afflicted (*saṃkliṣṭā*) in its stained state (*samalāvasthā*) and pure (*viśuddhā*) in its stainless state (*vimalāvasthā*). This aspect (*ākāra*) is to be known immediately after the explanation of the sixteenfold divisions, such as internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) and so forth.
Since the proof for that [distinction] was indicated immediately after the enumeration of the distinctions, he asks, following that exposition: "How is the proof to be understood?
In this regard, what is the object of proof?
It is the state of being essentially pure, despite being defiled by adventitious secondary afflictions.
Regarding that, with reference to the proof of the state of being afflicted, the first chapter says: "If this affliction did not exist, all embodied beings would be liberated.
Liberation is the abandonment of affliction.
And the abandonment of those afflictions occurs through the cultivation of the path.

In this regard, if the emptiness of phenomena exists even when the antidote has not yet arisen—by the force of the word "even," it is as if it had arisen—due to adventitious secondary afflictions; [then...]

It would not be defiled; for if that were so, because of the absence of defilement, all sentient beings would be liberated without effort. "Without effort" means without the application of an antidote (*pratipakṣa*).

Since there is no liberation for living beings without an antidote, one must necessarily admit that during the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), suchness (*tathatā*) is defiled by adventitious stains.
Thus, the division of emptiness into its defiled state is established.
To establish that mode of division, he says: "If it were not pure, effort would be fruitless."
This is connected with the phrase "of embodied beings.
Now, even when the antidote has arisen—the word "even" (api) implying as if it had not arisen—it would not be purified;
this being the case, the undertaking for the sake of liberation would be fruitless.
Even through the cultivation of the antidote, the removal of that impurity would not occur;
nor is liberation possible for one who possesses impurity,
nor is it accepted that the undertaking for the sake of liberation is fruitless.
Therefore, one must necessarily accept that the purification of emptiness results from the removal of adventitious secondary afflictions through the cultivation of their antidotes.
In this way, the differentiation of the purification of emptiness is established.
Here, it is "defiled" due to the apprehension of defiled phenomena, and "purified" due to the apprehension of purified phenomena.
Indeed, that [defilement or purification] is not held to be directly [identical with] emptiness, because emptiness is dependent upon phenomena (dharmaparatantra).
For this very reason, they say: "All embodied beings would be liberated."
In this context, the term "embodied beings" (*dehinaḥ*) refers precisely to that which is appropriated [by consciousness].
Otherwise, if defilement or purification were to belong directly to emptiness itself, what connection would there be with embodied beings?
For it is said that through the purification of emptiness, there is the purification of embodied beings, and through the defilement of emptiness, there is their defilement.
And if emptiness were defiled during the stage of an ordinary person and pure during the stage of an noble one, then this would be established:
"It is neither defiled nor non-defiled; it is neither pure nor impure."

Thus [it is asked]: how is it that it is neither afflicted nor impure? Because the two types of purity are indicated by the context. Regarding this very point, he cites scripture: "Because the mind is luminous by its very nature (*prakṛtyā prabhāsvaratvāt*). And here, it is the true nature of the mind (*cittadharmatā*) itself that is expressed by the word "mind."
Because it is the very characteristic of the mind,
how could it be neither afflicted nor pure? Thus, the two negations— “it is not afflicted” and “it is not pure”— are not understood as being applicable.
It has been taught that it is afflicted by adventitious afflictions (*kleśa*) and not by its own nature;
there is also scriptural authority for the statement that it is defiled by adventitious secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
Since a twofold division was stated by way of being defiled and purified, for what purpose is a fourfold division further proclaimed?

Some say it is for the sake of distinguishing between the mundane and supramundane paths: for the mundane path is defiled by the impurities of its own level, yet it is not inferior because it serves as their antidote;
whereas the supramundane path, though impure due to distinctions such as weak, medium, and so forth, is pure because it is untainted (*anāsrava*).
Emptiness is not like this.
It is said to be "not afflicted" (*akliṣṭa*).
Others say it is called "not impure" (*aśuddha*) for the sake of distinguishing it from the eyes and so forth;
for the eyes and other [faculties] are not afflicted because they are unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Nor are they called "impure" because they are pure by virtue of not having the nature of being with-outflows (*sāsrava*);

likewise, although that [undefiled] is said not to be afflicted, it is not called "impure. To explain the specific meaning of being wholesome yet with-outflows, he says: for the wholesome-with-outflows, because it is included within *saṃsāra*, is not afflicted.
And it is pure because its maturation is desirable;
the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is not like this,
for that is defiled during the state of being entered (*viṣṭāvasthā*), and thus is not purely [pure].
Thus, this exposition on the defilement and purification of the various divisions of emptiness is established.
The summary meaning of emptiness should be understood both by way of its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and its formal determination (*vyavasthāna*).
Therein, by way of characteristics, it is [to be understood] by way of the characteristic of non-existence and the characteristic of existence.
It is characterized by non-existence because of the statement "it is indeed the absence of ideation" (*iyābhāvo hautivacanāt*);
it is characterized by existence because of the statement "the existence of non-existence is the first discernment" (*abhāvasya ca bhāvaḥ prathamaḥ paricchedaḥ*);

it is characterized by being free from both existence and non-existence because of the statement "neither existence nor non-existence"; and it is characterized by being free from identity and difference.
And this is the characteristic of emptiness;
therefore, because it is stated that [emptiness] has no characteristic separate from unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*),
such is the summarized meaning according to its characteristics.

Regarding how the summarized meaning (*piṇḍārtha*) is to be understood from the perspective of systematic arrangement (*vyavasthāna*), he says: it is to be understood from the perspective of systematic arrangement, namely, the arrangement of synonyms (*paryāya*) and so forth.
This means: synonyms, their meaning, their distinctions, and their proof.

Furthermore, through the exposition of these four types of characteristics and so on—the characteristic of intrinsic nature, the characteristic of activity, the characteristic of affliction (*saṃkleśa*), and the characteristic of purification (*vyavadāna*)—the antidotes to the four kinds of secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) have been stated.
In that regard, the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) serves as the antidote to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
And that [conceptual construction] consists in the grasping of existence, non-existence, both, or their separateness and oneness.
Upon hearing the characteristic of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), those who lack resolute faith experience terror.
As its antidote, the characteristic of activity consists of:

the activity of the suchness of signs; the activity that is non-erroneous regarding suchness; the activity of abandoning all signs; the activity of abiding in the state of being the object of supramundane omniscience; and the activity of serving as the cause for the noble dharmas with respect to the focal object.

Thus, the characteristic of differentiation is taught so that those who are indolent—those who grasp at conceptual constructions—may dispel their laziness by merely hearing about the nature of emptiness.
Thus, in order to dispel the doubts of those who enjoy [the teachings] as to how defilement occurs and how purification occurs, the definition of the lineage (*gotra*) has been explained;
this concludes the commentary on the first chapter, "The Definition."
